newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Plessey plans to list in Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Plessey plans to list in Australia.

text.p: South African electronics group Plessey Corp Ltd said on Tuesday it plans to list on the Australian Stock Exchange in about three years and is still on the lookout for acquisitions in Australia and the Asia Pacific.

Last month, Plessey completed the purchase of the traffic systems, aerospace and communications divisions of AWA Ltd, which would form the bulk of the South African group's newly-formed Plessey Asia Pacific Pty Ltd.
Asked if Plessey planned to publicly list in Australia, Plessey group chief executive officer John Temple replied: "Yes, we will ... but it won't be for about three years."

Temple said the Australian listed company would be the Plessey Asia Pacific Pty Ltd business, which is 74 percent owned by Plessey Corp. The remaining 26 percent is owned by investment bank RMB Australia Ltd and Marcel Corporate Pty Ltd.
He said Plessey would sell down its interest in the Australian listed company, but no level had been set as yet.
Plessey also plans to expand through acquisition in Australia and in the Asia Pacific region, but any purchase would be small, Temple told reporters at a luncheon.
"I think we would have to wait until we are listed before we could buy anything major," Temple said.
Temple said he expected Plessey Corp to report sales turnover of about 1.40 billion rand for the year ended March 31, 1997, up from 1.04 billion a year earlier.

"I think we will grow to about 1.4 billion (rand) this year," Temple said. Just over a quarter of the group's sales are non-rand derived, Temple said he hopes this would grow to about 50 percent by the year 2000.
He said he expected the rand to continue to fall.
Plessey is 26 percent owned by South African mutual life insurer Sanlam.
Temple said he expected most of the loss-making former AWA businesses to turn into profitability in about a year, but added the aerospace business could take longer.

"We shall spend about a year on it, I don't think it would need any more time than that," Temple said in response to a question on how long it would take the recently acquired Australian operations to turn into profit.
